description: We’re Launch Window, a team building Mission Architect for the Space Mission Design Game challenge: a browser game where players design a space mission, then fly it live under budget, power and mass limits. I’m a  student developer who loves space and teaching through games. We’d love teammates with skills in game design, front-end (HTML/JS), space science or engineering, UI/visual design, or storytelling. All levels welcome. Join us!
summary: Mission Architect is a browser game where players design a complete robotic space mission and then fly it turn by turn. Players choose a destination, launch vehicle, spacecraft, engine, antenna, orbit and instruments under a fixed budget. Every choice has a cost in mass, power, money or risk. Then they run the mission live, balancing battery, data and communications while random events like solar flares and antenna faults force quick decisions. It turns the abstract trade-offs of mission design into something students can feel, and every result explains why the mission succeeded or failed.
details:
What it does: Players pick one of five destinations (the Moon, Mars, Venus, Europa or asteroid Bennu), each with its own mission objective. They build a spacecraft from a launch vehicle, bus, propulsion system, communications system, orbit and science instruments. A live spacecraft diagram updates as they choose, and a ledger tracks budget, launch mass and propellant.

How it works: Propellant is calculated with the rocket equation, so a harder destination or a less efficient engine means a much heavier launch. Once launched, each turn the player chooses Observe, Downlink or Recharge. Observing collects data but drains the battery. Data only scores once it is downlinked to Earth, and the amount depends on the antenna, orbit and distance. Random events such as solar flares, battery faults and micrometeoroids can destroy instruments or cost battery, and players decide under a countdown timer. Unspent budget becomes a flight reserve for fixes and upgrades.

Collaboration: The game includes an experimental online team mode for up to four players, each with a role. It only works in the Claude-hosted version. The version linked here is for solo play.

Learning: After each flight the game explains what happened, such as how much propellant the rocket equation required or why a brownout occurred. After a Europa mission it compares the player’s craft with the real Europa Clipper. A first-time tutorial and glossary explain terms like delta-v and Isp.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page with no external libraries.

Limits : Launch vehicle capacities and prices and the Europa Clipper figures are real. Spacecraft costs, instrument stats, power use, events and scoring are simplified game values, not engineering data. The game does not model planetary flybys or detailed orbital mechanics.
